question: What are Spring bean scopes?
title: Spring Bean Scopes Overview
direct_answer: Bean scope defines how many instances of a bean Spring creates and how long they live. The five scopes are: singleton (default — one per context), prototype (new per injection), request (one per HTTP request), session (one per HTTP session), application (one per ServletContext).

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know all five bean scopes and can explain when each is appropriate
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Only mentioning singleton and prototype, forgetting the three web scopes (request, session, application)
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the prototype-in-singleton problem and how Spring uses proxies to handle web scopes injected into singletons

sections.title: Bean Scopes Control Instance Lifecycle
sections.content:
**Bean scope** determines how many instances of a bean the Spring container creates and how long those instances live.

Think of it like a factory's production policy: do we make one reusable product that everyone shares (singleton), or do we manufacture a fresh one for every customer (prototype)? Spring offers five scopes. The first two work in any Spring app: **singleton** creates one shared instance per ApplicationContext, and **prototype** creates a new instance every time the bean is requested. The other three are **web-specific scopes** available only in Spring MVC or WebFlux: **request** scope creates one instance per HTTP request, **session** scope creates one instance per user session, and **application** scope creates one instance per ServletContext (shared across all users). Choosing the right scope prevents thread-safety issues, memory leaks, and subtle bugs where one user sees another user's data.

sections.content:
amber|singleton|~Default, one per context|Shared instance|Should be stateless|Created eagerly
blue|prototype|~New each request|getBean returns new object|Spring will not destroy it|Stateful helpers
emerald|request / session|~Web scopes|One per HTTP request|One per user session|Need a web context
violet|Rule of Thumb|~Match state to scope|Stateless to singleton|Stateful to prototype|Never store state in a singleton

sections.title: Defining Bean Scopes in Spring
When to Use Each Scope
sections.content:
Use **singleton** (the default) for stateless service classes like controllers, services, and repositories that hold no user-specific data. This is 95% of your beans.

Use **prototype** when a bean has mutable state that shouldn't be shared — for example, a PDF generator that builds a report step by step, or a command object that accumulates user input.

Use **request** scope for beans that hold data valid only for one HTTP request, like a cart being checked out or search filters.

Use **session** scope for user-specific data that persists across multiple requests, like shopping cart contents, user preferences, or authentication state.

Use **application** scope for global shared state across all users, like app-wide configuration or metrics — rare in practice.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Forgetting web scopes exist**: Freshers often think Spring only has singleton and prototype, missing that request, session, and application scopes are available in web apps.
- **Using singleton for stateful beans**: Storing user-specific data (like current cart items) in a singleton bean causes one user to see another user's data because the instance is shared across all threads.
- **Not using proxyMode for web scopes**: Injecting a request or session scoped bean into a singleton without proxyMode=TARGET_CLASS fails because Spring can't inject a short-lived bean into a long-lived one — you get a BeanCreationException at startup.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Singleton scope**: one shared instance per ApplicationContext, default for all beans, must be stateless for thread safety
**Prototype scope**: new instance created every time the bean is injected or retrieved via getBean(), Spring does not manage destruction lifecycle
**Request scope**: one instance per HTTP request, destroyed when the request completes, requires web environment
**Session scope**: one instance per user HTTP session, lives until session timeout or invalidation, perfect for user-specific data like shopping carts
**Application scope**: one instance per ServletContext, shared across all users and sessions, used for app-wide shared state
**Scoped proxies**: required when injecting shorter-lived scopes (request, session) into longer-lived beans (singleton) using proxyMode attribute
**Thread safety**: singleton beans are shared across threads, so any mutable state must be synchronized or avoided entirely

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Bean scope controls how many instances Spring creates and how long they live. There are five scopes. Singleton is the default — Spring makes one instance per ApplicationContext and reuses it everywhere. It's what you use for services and repositories because they're stateless. Prototype scope creates a new instance every time you inject it or call getBean. You'd use this for something with mutable state, like a report generator that builds data step by step. Then there are three web scopes. Request scope gives you one instance per HTTP request — it's created when the request starts and destroyed when it finishes. Session scope is one instance per user session, perfect for things like a shopping cart that lives across multiple requests. Application scope is one instance per ServletContext, shared by everyone — that's rare, maybe for app-wide config. One tricky thing is you can't just inject a request or session scoped bean into a singleton. You need to add proxyMode equals TARGET_CLASS so Spring creates a proxy that delegates to the current request or session instance. If you don't, the app won't start. The key insight is singleton beans must be stateless because they're shared across threads in a web server. If you store user-specific data in a singleton, one user will see another user's data. That's when you reach for prototype or session scope instead.

question: What is the singleton bean scope in Spring?
title: Spring Singleton Bean Scope
direct_answer: Singleton is the default scope — Spring creates exactly one instance per ApplicationContext and shares it wherever the bean is injected. It's ideal for stateless service classes like @Service and @Repository. Note: singleton scope is per context, not per JVM.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand the most commonly used scope and its boundaries
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying singleton means one instance per JVM — it's actually one per ApplicationContext, so multiple contexts can have separate singleton instances
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain why singleton beans must be stateless to be thread-safe in a multi-threaded web application

sections.title: Singleton Scope: One Shared Instance
sections.content:
**Singleton scope** is the default bean scope in Spring. When you annotate a class with @Service, @Repository, or @Component without specifying a scope, Spring creates exactly one instance of that bean per **ApplicationContext** and reuses it for every injection point.

Think of it like a shared tool in a workshop: instead of giving each worker their own hammer, everyone uses the same one from the toolbox. This is efficient because creating objects is expensive, and most service-layer beans don't need separate instances. The critical boundary is the **ApplicationContext**, not the JVM — if you run two Spring Boot apps in the same JVM, each has its own ApplicationContext and thus its own singleton instances. Singleton beans must be **stateless** (no mutable instance fields) because they're shared across all threads handling concurrent requests in a web server. If you store request-specific data in instance variables, you'll get data corruption and security bugs.

sections.content:
amber|What It Is|~One per container|The default scope|Shared everywhere|Cached after first build
blue|Not the GoF Singleton|~Per-context, not per-JVM|Two contexts equals two beans|Spring-managed|No private constructor
emerald|Must Be Stateless|~Shared means thread-shared|No mutable instance fields|Use locals and params|Else race conditions
rose|Watch Out|~State bugs|Mutable field shared|Prototype-in-singleton trap|Use ObjectProvider

sections.title: Singleton Bean in Action
When to Use Singleton Scope
sections.content:
Use singleton scope for **stateless service classes** — beans that perform operations without storing mutable state in instance variables. Examples: @Service classes that orchestrate business logic, @Repository classes that interact with databases, @RestController classes that handle HTTP requests, and @Component utility classes like validators or formatters. These beans typically have dependencies injected via constructor and use only local variables within methods. Local variables are allocated per method call on the call stack, so they're naturally thread-safe. Singleton is the right choice for 95% of your beans because it's memory-efficient and Spring manages the lifecycle automatically.

Avoid singleton when you need to store request-specific or user-specific data — that's when you need prototype, request, or session scope instead.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Thinking singleton means one per JVM**: Freshers often say singleton scope creates one instance per JVM, but it's actually one per ApplicationContext. If you have a parent-child context hierarchy or run multiple Spring apps in one JVM (like in integration tests), you'll have multiple singleton instances.
- **Storing mutable state in instance variables**: Adding a field like private String currentUser to a singleton service causes thread-safety bugs. Thread A sets it to Alice, then Thread B sets it to Bob before Thread A's request finishes — now Thread A sees Bob's data.
- **Expecting singleton behavior across restarts**: Singleton instances are created when the ApplicationContext starts and destroyed on shutdown. They're not persisted, so state is lost between application restarts.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Default scope**: every bean is singleton unless you explicitly specify a different scope using the @Scope annotation
**One per ApplicationContext**: the singleton boundary is the Spring container, not the JVM or classloader
**Shared across threads**: in a web app, the same singleton instance handles requests from multiple threads concurrently
**Stateless requirement**: singleton beans must not store mutable request-specific or user-specific data in instance fields to avoid data corruption
**Thread-safe by design**: use only final fields injected via constructor and local variables within methods for automatic thread safety
**Lifecycle management**: Spring calls @PostConstruct after construction and @PreDestroy before shutdown, both exactly once per singleton
**Memory efficient**: reusing one instance across thousands of requests saves memory and avoids garbage collection overhead

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Singleton is the default scope in Spring. It means Spring creates exactly one instance of the bean per ApplicationContext and reuses that same instance everywhere it's injected. So if you have an OrderService annotated with at-Service, Spring creates one OrderService object when the context starts up, and every controller or other service that needs it gets that same instance. It's important to know the boundary is the ApplicationContext, not the JVM. If you run two Spring apps in the same JVM, each has its own ApplicationContext, so you'd actually have two OrderService instances — one per app. The big reason singleton is the default is efficiency. Creating objects is expensive, and most beans don't need separate instances. But there's a critical rule: singleton beans must be stateless. That means no mutable instance fields storing request-specific data. In a web app, the same singleton instance is handling requests from multiple threads at the same time. If you put something like private String currentUser as a field, Thread A sets it to Alice, then Thread B sets it to Bob before Thread A finishes — now Thread A sees Bob's data. That's a security bug. The safe pattern is to use only final fields injected via constructor, and keep request-specific data in local variables within methods. Local variables live on the stack, so each thread has its own copy automatically.

question: What is the default scope for Spring beans and why?
title: Why Singleton Is the Default Spring Bean Scope
direct_answer: The default scope is singleton because most Spring beans are stateless services where sharing a single instance across the entire application is safe and efficient. Creating new instances for every injection would waste memory and CPU on redundant object creation when one shared instance can serve all consumers.

sections.title: Why Singleton is Spring's Default Bean Scope
sections.content:
**Singleton scope** means Spring creates exactly one instance of the bean per container and shares it across all injection points. It's the default because typical Spring applications follow a **stateless service architecture**: your service layer, repository layer, and controllers don't hold per-request data in instance fields.

They're just collections of methods that operate on parameters and return results. Think of a calculator—you don't need a separate calculator for each math problem; one calculator can solve them all because it doesn't remember previous calculations. A **UserService** with methods like findById or updateEmail is stateless—it doesn't store which user it's currently processing. Since these beans are stateless, sharing one instance is perfectly thread-safe. Spring runs in **servlet containers** where hundreds of concurrent HTTP requests might be executing simultaneously. If Spring defaulted to prototype scope, it would create hundreds of UserService instances all doing the same job, wasting heap memory and GC pressure. Singleton scope gives you **performance** (one allocation), **memory efficiency** (one object in the heap), and **simplicity** (no lifecycle management). The alternative would be absurd: imagine creating a new OrderRepository instance for every single injection point in your application.

sections.content:
amber|The Default|~singleton scope|One instance per context|Used if you set nothing|Shared everywhere

emerald|Safe Because|~Services are stateless|No mutable fields|Logic uses params/locals|Thread-safe by design
rose|Watch Out|~If you add state|Shared across threads|Race conditions|Change scope or remove state

sections.title: Singleton Bean Shared Across Multiple Consumers
When Singleton Scope is Appropriate
sections.content:
Use singleton scope (the default) for any **stateless bean**: services, repositories, controllers, validators, mappers, utilities. A bean is stateless if it doesn't store per-request or per-user data in instance fields. For example, a PaymentService that calls external APIs is stateless even though it has a WebClient field—that field is the same for all requests, not request-specific data. Configuration beans like DataSource or RestTemplate are perfect singletons—you want one shared connection pool, not hundreds. **Thread-local** patterns also work with singleton: if your bean stores data in ThreadLocal variables, each thread gets its own copy even though the bean instance is shared.

Avoid singleton only when you need **per-request state** (use request scope), **per-session state** (use session scope), or **per-operation mutable state** (use prototype). In 95% of Spring applications, every bean you write should be singleton because Spring encourages a stateless service-oriented design.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Storing Request Data in Singleton Fields**: Freshers sometimes add instance fields like private String currentUserId to a singleton service and update it during request processing. This is catastrophic—concurrent requests will overwrite each other's data. Always pass request-specific data as method parameters.
- **Thinking Singleton Means Single-Threaded**: Singleton scope doesn't mean only one thread can use the bean at a time. Hundreds of threads can call methods on the same singleton instance concurrently, so any mutable shared state would cause race conditions. Singleton plus stateless equals thread-safe.
- **Using Prototype Without Reason**: Some freshers mark beans as prototype thinking it's safer, but prototype creates a new instance per injection (not per method call), increases memory usage, and is usually wrong unless the bean holds mutable per-use state.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Singleton Scope**: One instance per Spring container—the instance is created once and shared across all injection points and requests
**Stateless Services**: Most Spring beans are stateless (no mutable instance fields holding request data), making singleton safe and efficient
**Thread Safety**: Singleton beans are accessed by multiple threads concurrently in servlet containers—statelessness ensures no race conditions
**Memory Efficiency**: Creating one instance instead of thousands reduces heap usage and garbage collection pressure in high-traffic applications
**Performance**: Singleton avoids repeated object instantiation and dependency injection overhead for every request or injection point
**Design Philosophy**: Spring promotes service-oriented architecture where business logic lives in stateless method implementations, not object state
**When to Use Prototype**: Only when you need mutable per-use state (like builders) or per-request state (though request scope is usually better)

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: The default scope is singleton because most beans in a Spring application are stateless services, and sharing one instance is both safe and efficient. A typical Spring app has services, repositories, and controllers that don't store any per-request data in instance fields. They just have methods that take parameters and return results. Since these beans don't hold state, there's no problem with multiple threads using the same instance concurrently—it's completely thread-safe. If Spring defaulted to prototype scope instead, it would create a new service instance for every injection point. Imagine having hundreds of UserService instances when one can serve the entire application. That's a huge waste of memory and CPU cycles. Spring runs in servlet containers where you might have hundreds of HTTP requests executing at the same time, all calling methods on the same singleton beans. This is fine because the beans are stateless. The singleton pattern gives you memory efficiency, better performance, and simpler lifecycle management. You'd only use a different scope like prototype or request when you need per-use mutable state or per-request session data, which is rare. The vast majority of beans you write should be singleton because that's what the stateless service architecture is all about.

question: What is the prototype bean scope and when do you use it?
title: Spring Prototype Bean Scope
direct_answer: Prototype scope creates a new bean instance every time it's injected or requested via getBean(). Use it for stateful beans, command objects, or any bean where sharing an instance would cause correctness issues. Spring does NOT call @PreDestroy on prototype beans.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand when singleton scope is inappropriate and prototype is necessary
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing that Spring doesn't manage the destruction lifecycle of prototype beans — no @PreDestroy callback is invoked
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the prototype-in-singleton trap and all three solutions: ObjectProvider, @Lookup method injection, and ApplicationContext.getBean()

sections.title: Prototype Scope: Fresh Instance Every Time
sections.content:
**Prototype scope** tells Spring to create a new bean instance every single time the bean is injected or retrieved via ApplicationContext.getBean(). Unlike singleton (one shared instance), prototype is like ordering a custom-made sandwich — you get a fresh one each time. This is essential for **stateful beans** that accumulate data during their lifetime, like a PDF report generator that builds content step by step, or a command object that collects user input across multiple method calls.

The key difference: Spring hands you the instance and then forgets about it. Spring does NOT manage the destruction lifecycle of prototype beans, so **@PreDestroy methods are never called**. You're responsible for cleanup. Prototype solves the thread-safety problem for stateful objects, but introduces the **prototype-in-singleton trap**: if you inject a prototype bean into a singleton via constructor, you only get one instance (created at singleton construction time), defeating the purpose.

sections.title: Prototype Scope at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|What It Is|~New bean each time|Per getBean or injection|Never cached|Good for stateful objects
blue|Lifecycle Gap|~Spring steps back|Creates and wires it|No destroy callback|You manage cleanup
emerald|When to Use|~Stateful, short-lived|Per-request builders|Command objects|Non-thread-safe helpers
rose|The Classic Trap|~Inside a singleton|Injected once equals one instance|Use @Lookup / ObjectProvider|Or a scoped proxy

sections.title: Defining and Using Prototype Beans
When to Use Prototype Scope
sections.content: Use prototype scope when you need **stateful beans** where each usage requires isolated mutable state. Examples: a report generator that accumulates data before rendering, a shopping cart being built up during checkout, a multi-step wizard that collects user input across pages, or a command object that validates and processes form data. Prototype is also useful for **expensive objects that vary by request**, like database connections from a pool (though modern connection pools handle this internally). Another use case is **beans with different configurations per usage** — imagine a file processor that needs different output formats (PDF, CSV, JSON) and you configure it per request. The key signal you need prototype: if reusing the bean instance would cause one operation to see data from a previous operation, or if two concurrent operations would corrupt each other's state.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Injecting prototype into singleton via constructor**: The most common mistake. If you inject a prototype bean into a singleton's constructor, Spring creates one prototype instance at startup and reuses it forever — you lost the prototype behavior. You must use ObjectProvider, @Lookup method injection, or getBean() to get a fresh instance each time.
- **Expecting Spring to call @PreDestroy**: Spring does not track prototype beans after creation, so @PreDestroy methods are never invoked. If your prototype bean holds resources like file handles or database connections, you must manually close them — there's no automatic cleanup.
- **Using prototype when you need request or session scope**: Freshers sometimes use prototype for web-scoped data like user sessions. That's wrong because you'll get a new instance on every injection, not one per request or session. Use the appropriate web scope instead.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **New instance every time**: Spring creates a fresh bean instance on every call to getBean() or every injection point where the bean is used
**Stateful beans**: prototype scope is designed for beans with mutable state that shouldn't be shared across uses
**No destruction lifecycle**: Spring does not call @PreDestroy on prototype beans — you must manually clean up resources
**Prototype-in-singleton trap**: injecting a prototype bean into a singleton via constructor gives you only one instance, defeating the purpose
**ObjectProvider solution**: inject ObjectProvider<YourBean> into the singleton, then call getObject() to get a fresh prototype instance each time
**@Lookup method injection**: annotate an abstract method with @Lookup, Spring generates a subclass that returns a new instance on every call
**ApplicationContext.getBean()**: directly call context.getBean(YourBean.class) to retrieve a new prototype instance, though this couples you to Spring APIs

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Prototype scope means Spring creates a brand new instance every time you ask for the bean. If you inject it five times or call getBean five times, you get five separate objects. You'd use this when your bean has mutable state that shouldn't be shared. For example, imagine an invoice generator that accumulates line items and totals as you add products. If that's a singleton, multiple threads would corrupt each other's invoices. Making it prototype solves that — each invoice generation gets its own isolated instance. There's an important gotcha though. Spring doesn't manage the destruction lifecycle of prototype beans. If you have a @PreDestroy method, it's never called. So if your prototype bean opens a file or database connection, you have to close it yourself — Spring won't do it for you. The other big trap is the prototype-in-singleton problem. If you inject a prototype bean into a singleton via constructor, you only get one instance created at startup, and that defeats the whole point. The solution is to use ObjectProvider. Instead of injecting the prototype bean directly, you inject ObjectProvider of that bean type. Then inside your method, you call provider dot getObject to get a fresh instance every time. Another option is @Lookup method injection, where you declare an abstract method and Spring generates a subclass that returns a new instance on every call. The key thing to remember is prototype is for stateful beans where sharing an instance would cause bugs or data corruption.

items: New instance per injection: every @Autowired point that declares a prototype bean gets its own copy.
New instance per getBean(): calling applicationContext.getBean(Type.class) on a prototype also creates a fresh instance.
No @PreDestroy: Spring doesn't manage prototype bean destruction — release resources manually if needed.
ObjectProvider<T> as a factory: injecting ObjectProvider<ReportBuilder> lets a singleton get a new prototype on every getObject() call.

beats.text: In our Spring Boot 3.2 app, ReportBuilder is @Scope("prototype"). ReportService injects ObjectProvider<ReportBuilder> via constructor. Each call to generateReport() calls builderProvider.getObject() to get a fresh, empty builder, builds the report, and discards the builder. production trap: if ReportService had @Autowired ReportBuilder directly, Spring would inject one prototype at startup and ReportService would reuse that same builder for every report — corrupting results for concurrent requests.

items: Don't @Autowired a prototype directly into a singleton — it defeats the purpose. Use ObjectProvider or @Lookup method injection.
You're responsible for cleanup of prototype beans — if they hold resources like file handles, close them explicitly.

speakable_v2.cap: Prototype gives you a truly fresh bean, but only if you fetch it through ObjectProvider — direct @Autowired in a singleton is a trap.

question: What are request and session scopes in Spring?
title: Request and Session Scopes in Spring
direct_answer: Request scope creates one bean instance per HTTP request — bean is created when the request starts and destroyed when it ends. Session scope creates one bean instance per HTTP session — lives for the user's session lifetime. Both require proxyMode equals TARGET_CLASS when injected into singletons.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand web-specific scopes and how they differ from singleton and prototype
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing that proxyMode is required when injecting request or session scoped beans into singleton beans, causing startup errors
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give a realistic session scope example like shopping cart or user preferences, and explain how the scoped proxy delegates to the current request or session instance

sections.title: Web Scopes for HTTP Request and Session Data
sections.content:
**Request scope** and **session scope** are web-specific bean scopes available only in Spring MVC or WebFlux applications. Request scope creates one bean instance per HTTP request — the bean is instantiated when the request starts and destroyed when the response is sent.

Think of it like a notepad you use during one phone call and throw away afterwards. **Session scope** creates one bean instance per user HTTP session — the bean lives from the user's first request (when the session is created) until session timeout or logout. It's like a file folder you keep for each customer containing their preferences and history. These scopes solve the problem of storing temporary user-specific data without making your singleton services stateful. The critical detail: when you inject a request or session scoped bean into a singleton, Spring can't directly inject the short-lived bean into the long-lived one. You must add **proxyMode equals TARGET_CLASS** to the scope annotation. Spring then injects a proxy that delegates to the current request or session instance at runtime.

sections.title: Request vs Session Scope
sections.content:
amber|request scope|~One per HTTP request|New for each request|Dies when request ends|Holds per-call data
blue|session scope|~One per user session|Spans many requests|Dies on session end|Holds per-user data
emerald|Requirement|~Web context only|Needs a web app|Fails in a plain context|Use a scoped proxy to inject
violet|Inject Into Singleton|~proxyMode needed|TARGET_CLASS proxy|Resolves the real bean per request|Else stale data

sections.title: Request vs Session Scope
sections.content:
| Aspect | Request Scope | Session Scope |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Lifecycle | Created per HTTP request, destroyed when response sent | Created per user session, destroyed on session timeout or logout |
| Typical use case | Search filters, form data, request-specific context | Shopping cart, user preferences, authentication state |
| Annotation | @RequestScope or @Scope with WebApplicationContext.SCOPE_REQUEST | @SessionScope or @Scope with WebApplicationContext.SCOPE_SESSION |
| Shared across requests | No, each request gets its own instance | Yes, same instance across all requests in one session |
| Memory footprint | Low, destroyed quickly after each request | Higher, lives until session expires (typically 30 minutes idle) |

sections.title: Request bean injected directly - stale data
Scoped proxy resolves per request
When to Use Request and Session Scopes
sections.content:
Use **request scope** for data that's valid only for the duration of one HTTP request. Examples: user search filters that customize query results, a temporary shopping cart being checked out, request-specific audit context (user ID, correlation ID, IP address), or form submission data that's validated and processed in one request. Request scope keeps this data isolated so concurrent requests don't interfere with each other.

Use **session scope** for user-specific data that needs to persist across multiple requests. Examples: shopping cart contents that the user builds up over several pages, user preferences like language or theme that affect multiple requests, wizard state for multi-step forms, or authentication principal information. Session scope is cheaper than storing this data in a database or distributed cache for every request, but be mindful of memory usage — sessions can live for 30 minutes after the last request.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Forgetting proxyMode when injecting into singletons**: The most common error. If you inject a request or session scoped bean into a singleton service without proxyMode equals TARGET_CLASS, Spring throws a BeanCreationException at startup saying it can't inject a shorter-lived bean into a longer-lived one. The proxy is essential because it delays resolution until runtime.
- **Using session scope for data that should be in the database**: Freshers sometimes store things like order history or saved addresses in session scope. Sessions expire, servers restart, and in a load-balanced environment, session data might not replicate. Persistent data belongs in the database.
- **Not invalidating sessions on logout**: Session scoped beans live until you explicitly call HttpSession.invalidate(). If you don't invalidate the session when the user logs out, the old session can be hijacked or consume memory unnecessarily.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Request scope lifecycle**: bean instance created when HTTP request starts, destroyed when response is sent, one per concurrent request
**Session scope lifecycle**: bean instance created on first access in a session, destroyed on session timeout or HttpSession.invalidate(), shared across all requests from the same user
**proxyMode requirement**: must use proxyMode equals TARGET_CLASS or INTERFACES when injecting request or session scoped beans into singletons to avoid BeanCreationException
**Scoped proxy mechanism**: Spring injects a CGLIB proxy that delegates method calls to the actual request or session instance at runtime based on current thread context
**Thread safety**: request and session scoped beans are naturally thread-safe because each request thread or session has its own instance
**Realistic session example**: shopping cart is the classic use case — stores items added by the user across multiple pages, persists between requests, cleared on checkout or logout
**Memory considerations**: session scoped beans consume memory until session expiration (default 30 minutes idle), so avoid storing large objects or too many fields

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Request and session scopes are web-specific scopes for storing HTTP-related data. Request scope creates one bean instance per HTTP request. It's born when the request comes in and destroyed when the response goes out. You'd use this for things like search filters or form data that's only relevant for one request. Session scope creates one instance per user session — it lives from the user's first request until they log out or the session times out, usually 30 minutes of inactivity. Session scope is perfect for a shopping cart. The user adds items across multiple requests as they browse, and the cart instance holds all those items until checkout. The tricky part is you can't just inject a request or session scoped bean into a singleton service. Spring would complain at startup because you're trying to inject a short-lived bean into a long-lived one. The solution is to add proxyMode equals TARGET_CLASS to the scope annotation. That tells Spring to inject a proxy instead of the real bean. The proxy looks like the bean but delegates method calls to the actual request or session instance at runtime. So when your singleton service calls a method on the cart, the proxy figures out which session the current request belongs to and forwards the call to that session's cart instance. Without the proxy, you'd get a BeanCreationException saying the scopes are incompatible. One pitfall is don't store things in session scope that belong in a database, like order history. Sessions expire and servers restart, so you'd lose that data. Session scope is for temporary user-specific state that only matters during the active session.

groups.heading: Request scope
groups.text: One bean instance per HTTP request. It's created when the request arrives and destroyed when the response is sent. Each request gets its own instance, so storing per-request data is completely thread-safe. Useful for request context objects you want available throughout the filter-controller-service chain.

groups.heading: Session scope
groups.text: One bean instance per user HTTP session. It survives across multiple requests from the same user and lives until the session expires. The classic use case is a shopping cart — items added across several page visits persist in the same bean instance.

items: Use request scope when you need per-request data flowing through multiple layers without passing it as method parameters.
Use session scope for user-specific stateful data that must survive across multiple requests — like a multi-step checkout.
Don't use session scope in stateless REST APIs with JWT — there's no server-side session to bind to.

beats.text: gotcha: both scopes need proxyMode=ScopedProxyMode.TARGET_CLASS when injected into a singleton. Without it, the singleton grabs one instance at startup — always the wrong request's or session's data. The proxy tells Spring to look up the real scoped bean per-request or per-session each time a method is called on it.

question: What is the problem with injecting a prototype bean into a singleton in Spring?
title: Prototype Bean in Singleton Problem
direct_answer: When a prototype bean is injected into a singleton via constructor or field injection, Spring creates the prototype only once—when the singleton is instantiated. The singleton then holds that single prototype instance for its entire lifetime, effectively making the prototype behave like a singleton and defeating the purpose of prototype scope.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of how Spring resolves dependencies at container startup and the lifecycle interaction between different bean scopes
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Assuming Spring automatically creates a new prototype instance each time the singleton uses it, when in reality the injection happens only once at singleton creation time
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Demonstrate knowledge of all three solutions: ObjectProvider for lazy programmatic lookup, method injection with @Lookup, and scoped proxies with proxyMode in @Scope

sections.title: The Prototype-in-Singleton Injection Problem
sections.content:
Spring's **dependency injection** happens at bean creation time, not at method invocation time. When you inject a **prototype bean** into a **singleton bean**, Spring resolves that dependency once—when it creates the singleton during application startup. The singleton stores a reference to that single prototype instance and reuses it forever.

Think of it like a vending machine (singleton) that's supposed to dispense a fresh cup (prototype) each time, but instead it was built with one permanent cup attached to it. Every customer gets the same cup. The prototype bean loses its per-use semantics and effectively becomes a singleton. This is problematic when the prototype holds **stateful data** like user-specific information or per-request context. If UserSession is prototype-scoped but injected into a singleton OrderService, all users would share the same UserSession instance—a serious bug. The root cause is Spring's **eager dependency resolution**: it wires all dependencies when the container starts, not when your code calls a method.

sections.title: Prototype-in-Singleton at a Glance
sections.content:
rose|The Problem|~Injection happens once|Singleton built one time|Prototype injected once|Same instance reused
amber|Why It Surprises|~You expect new each call|But the field is fixed|Scope ignored after wiring|A silent bug
blue|Fix 1: ObjectProvider|~Ask per use|provider.getObject()|Fresh prototype each call|Clean and typed
emerald|Fix 2: @Lookup|~Method injection|Spring overrides the method|Returns a new bean|Or use a scoped proxy

sections.title: Prototype Injection Problem and Solution with ObjectProvider
When This Problem Occurs
sections.content:
This issue appears when you mix **stateful prototype beans** with **singleton services**. Common scenarios: (1) A prototype bean holding per-request user context or session data gets injected into a singleton REST controller—every HTTP request would see the same user context. (2) A prototype bean with per-operation metrics or timing data is injected into a singleton service—metrics from different operations get mixed together. (3) A prototype bean acting as a factory or builder with mutable state is cached in a singleton—concurrent threads would corrupt each other's state. The problem doesn't occur if the prototype bean is truly stateless (no fields that change), but then you should just use singleton scope instead.

Use ObjectProvider, @Lookup method injection, or scoped proxies whenever you need fresh prototype instances from a singleton.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Expecting Magic Prototype Behavior**: Freshers assume that marking a bean as prototype automatically makes Spring create new instances whenever the bean is used, even after injection. Spring only honors prototype scope at injection time—if you inject it once into a singleton, you get one instance forever.
- **Using ApplicationContext.getBean() Everywhere**: Some freshers discover getBean() as a solution and then call applicationContext.getBean(PrototypeBean.class) scattered throughout their code, turning Spring into a service locator anti-pattern. Use ObjectProvider instead—it's type-safe and designed for this exact scenario.
- **Not Understanding When Prototype Is Needed**: Freshers mark beans as prototype without justification. If your bean has no mutable state, singleton is always better—prototype scope is only for beans that hold per-use or per-request state that can't be shared.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Injection Time**: Spring resolves dependencies when creating the singleton, not when methods are called—prototype is instantiated once and cached
**Scope Mismatch**: A longer-lived scope (singleton) holding a shorter-lived scope (prototype) always causes the shorter scope to be promoted to the longer scope's lifetime
**ObjectProvider<T>**: Spring's recommended way to get fresh prototype instances programmatically—call getObject() each time you need a new instance
**@Lookup Method Injection**: Annotate an abstract method returning the prototype type and Spring generates a subclass that returns a new instance per call
**Scoped Proxy**: Use @Scope(value="prototype", proxyMode=ScopedProxyMode.TARGET_CLASS) to inject a proxy that delegates to fresh instances
**Stateless Beans Use Singleton**: If your prototype bean has no mutable fields, you don't need prototype scope—just use the default singleton
**Thread Safety**: Prototype beans with state are thread-safe by design (each use gets its own instance) but lose that safety when stuck in a singleton

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: The problem is that Spring injects dependencies when it creates the singleton bean, not when you call methods on it. So if you inject a prototype bean into a singleton using constructor or field injection, Spring creates that prototype instance once during application startup. The singleton holds onto that single instance forever, effectively making the prototype behave like a singleton. Let's say you have a RequestProcessor that's prototype-scoped because it holds request-specific data like a request ID. If you inject it directly into a singleton OrderService, every order processed by that service will use the same RequestProcessor instance with the same request ID. That defeats the whole purpose of prototype scope. The cleanest solution is to use ObjectProvider. Instead of injecting RequestProcessor directly, you inject ObjectProvider of RequestProcessor. Then in your method, you call provider dot getObject to get a fresh instance each time. Spring also supports at-Lookup method injection where you define an abstract method that returns the prototype, and Spring implements it to return new instances. You can also use scoped proxies by setting proxyMode equals TARGET_CLASS in the at-Scope annotation, which makes Spring inject a proxy that delegates to fresh instances. The key thing to remember is that prototype scope only works at injection time—once injected, it's just a regular object reference.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 app with @Service, @Repository, and constructor injection
speakable_v2.hook: You marked it prototype, but the singleton only asked for it once — now everyone's sharing the 'fresh' instance you thought you'd get.

beats.text: The prototype-in-singleton problem is when a prototype-scoped bean is @Autowired directly into a singleton. Spring injects the prototype once — when it creates the singleton — and the singleton holds that same instance for its entire lifetime. Prototype semantics are completely lost. It behaves as if the bean were singleton.

Spring's injection wiring runs once at startup. The singleton asks for a TaskProcessor, Spring creates one prototype instance, injects it, and that's the end of injection for that field. There's no mechanism to re-inject the field on every method call — unless you explicitly design for it.

items: Wrong pattern: @Autowired TaskProcessor processor in a singleton — one prototype instance for the singleton's lifetime.
ObjectProvider fix (recommended): inject ObjectProvider<TaskProcessor> and call getObject() each time you need a fresh one.
@Lookup fix: annotate a protected abstract method — Spring overrides it to return a new prototype on every call.
ApplicationContext.getBean() fix: works but it's the Service Locator anti-pattern — avoid in production code.

beats.text: In our Spring Boot 3.2 app, TaskService is singleton. TaskProcessor is @Scope("prototype") because it holds per-task mutable state. If TaskService @Autowires TaskProcessor directly, every task shares the same processor — state from task A bleeds into task B. The fix: inject ObjectProvider<TaskProcessor>. Each call to processorProvider.getObject() creates a brand new TaskProcessor. candidates miss: @Lookup also works — you declare protected abstract TaskProcessor createProcessor(); and Spring generates an implementation that creates a fresh prototype each time.

items: The bug is silent — Spring doesn't warn you that the prototype is being degraded to singleton behavior.
Don't use ApplicationContext.getBean() as the fix in your service layer — it's the Service Locator anti-pattern and makes testing harder.

speakable_v2.cap: Direct @Autowired of a prototype into a singleton silently breaks prototype semantics — always use ObjectProvider or @Lookup to get a fresh instance.
